name: STRN homepage: the Sports Tech Research Network landing page
title: STRN homepage: the Sports Tech Research Network landing page
answer: This is the landing page of the Sports Tech Research Network, or STRN, a non-profit that connects sports, tech and business scientists with research-driven industry. Its most useful point is that STRN positions itself as a matchmaker between academia, industry and sports field practice, aiming to create, bring to market and implement sports technology that is trustworthy and effective because it is based on science. It also states that sports, health and medical technology need not be separate fields but can sit on a continuum.

sections.body: This is the home page of the Sports Tech Research Network, published by STRN itself. It is a short organisational landing page rather than a report, study or article, and it describes what the network is, who it is for and how to take part. No publication date is stated on the page, which was harvested on 28 September 2026. The page states that STRN is an initiative of Victoris, the sports innovation consortium at Ghent University in Belgium, in collaboration with the non-profit organisation SportaMundi. It also carries cookie, privacy and website analytics notices, which are boilerplate rather than substantive content.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: STRN describes itself as a non-profit initiative that brings together research-driven professionals from academia, industry and sports field practice. The stated common goal is to create, bring to market and implement sports technology solutions that are trustworthy and effective because they are based on science. The network says it facilitates multi-disciplinary collaborations that result in new products and services reaching the market. It then addresses several audiences. Scientists who care about inspiring collaborations and real-life solutions as well as excellent research and publications are invited. People who want closer involvement with the academic community, or with field practitioners who use effective solutions, are offered help. Those interested in research, implementation and open innovation projects for the benefit of sports and society are invited to become members. Anyone with prototypes or related findings who wants to bring something to market is asked to make contact, with the promise of help defining strategies and partners. Those looking to spot the best solutions or to co-develop them are asked to contribute. STRN also promotes bringing sports technology, health technology and medical technology together, arguing that these do not have to be distinct and can form a continuum.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The text gives no numbers, statistics, dates or definitions. The positions it does state are that STRN is a non-profit initiative, that its goal is trustworthy and effective sports technology based on science, that it facilitates multi-disciplinary collaborations leading to products and services on the market, that sports, health and medical technology can be treated as a continuum rather than distinct areas, and that STRN is an initiative of Victoris at Ghent University in collaboration with SportaMundi.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: The source never mentions artificial intelligence, so it offers no direct evidence about AI methods, tools or adoption in sport. A reader following AI in this industry would use it only as a pointer to an organisation that positions itself between academic research and commercial sports technology, and as an example of how that field frames trustworthy, science-based solutions and research translation. It can support context about who brokers research and industry in sports tech, but it cannot support any claim about AI specifically.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Sports

sections.body: This is a membership-oriented landing page, promotional in tone and thin on substance. It states no date, cites no research, lists no publications and names no quality framework, so it does not support the claim on the citing page that STRN published a peer-reviewed framework for assessing sports tech. It contains nothing about artificial intelligence, nothing about specific sports or products, and no evidence of outcomes. The only other content is cookie, privacy and analytics boilerplate.
